title: The potter's house (Jeremiah 18:1–6)
hookLine: the clay spoils, and the potter makes it again into another vessel

lines: GO DOWN TO THE POTTER'S HOUSE.
cards: A pottery class, week one. The wheel is spinning, a student's hands are wet, and the bowl is rising, actually rising. I'm good at this, she thinks.
Then one thumb presses a little too hard, and the whole wall wobbles, folds, and collapses into a lump. The teacher doesn't sigh and throw it out.
She squashes it back into a ball, wets it, slaps it back on the wheel, and says: again. God once sent Jeremiah to watch exactly that. Not to a temple, not to a palace.

teach.b: The word comes to Jeremiah: get up and go down to the potter's house, and there I'll let you hear my words. In the King James Bible: "Then I went down to the potter's house, and, behold, he wrought a work on the wheels."
The King James says wheels, plural. Jeremiah watches, and it goes wrong.

"And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it." Marred: spoiled, ruined. The potter doesn't throw the clay away.

teach.h: HE MADE IT AGAIN, ANOTHER VESSEL.
teach.b: He keeps it in his hands and starts again, making another vessel, not necessarily the same one. Then God speaks: "Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel."
This can sound frightening: God can do whatever he likes with us. And the next verses do warn: if a nation does evil, its future can change.
But they also say the opposite: if a nation God has warned turns from its evil, God will relent. The clay's story isn't fixed. That's the hope in it.
One more detail. In the very next chapter, God sends Jeremiah to buy a finished clay jar and smash it in front of the city's leaders. A finished jar can't be reshaped.

teach.h: AS THE CLAY IS IN THE POTTER'S HAND.
teach.b: Some Christians hear this as a picture of grace: as long as you're still on the wheel, the potter can start again.

how: Christians often use the image of the potter and the clay in prayer and song, asking God to reshape them, and Jeremiah 18 is read in services focused on repentance and new beginnings.

games.q: you're the potter. the pot on your wheel has just collapsed. what do you do?
o: throw the clay away and get new clay.
make it again into another vessel.
games.why: "so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter." same clay, new shape.

practice: Think of one thing you spoiled, a conversation that went wrong, a project you abandoned, a promise you broke, a relationship you bent out of shape, and picture it as clay that collapsed on the wheel.
Notice the sinking feeling, then notice that the clay is still there, not thrown away, and wonder what starting again might look like: not the same thing, but another vessel, maybe a better one.
If you pray, you can place it in the potter's hands.

wordCard.voice: Vessel. What the clay becomes in the potter's hands, spoiled once and remade into another, as long as it's still soft enough to shape.

orig.note: Hebrew: potter, one who forms. the same root as formed in Genesis 2:7.

carryVoice: Your line: the potter starts again. Soft clay can still change. That's day four hundred seventy-four.
